Buddhist Psychology and the Nature of the Mind

Everything we experience arrives through the mind, yet most of us never examine it. In the Lamrim and Abhidharma tradition, the mind (sems) is defined by clarity and knowing. Feeling, perception, intention, and attention are mental factors that color how the mind engages with its objects. The tradition catalogues 51 such factors, some virtuous, such as faith and compassion, and some afflictive, such as anger, pride, and ignorance. Psychological health means knowing which factors are operating and where they are pulling the mind.

The mind has no beginning. Each moment of consciousness arises from the moment before it, so habits and emotional patterns carry forward. Because the mind is a flow shaped by its own prior states, it can be reshaped through deliberate training.

Ordinary experience presents a self that seems solid and independent. The tradition holds that this self is merely imputed, designated on the basis of body and mind, and cannot be found as a separate entity. Clinging to the self as it appears is the root of suffering, because that self becomes the object of fear, craving, and pride.

Suffering arises from afflictions, which arise from ignorance of how phenomena exist. Freedom is therefore an inner achievement, available to anyone who examines and changes their own mental habits.

At its subtlest level, the mind’s fundamental nature is clear light: clarity and knowing in pure form. Its afflictions are adventitious, like clouds passing across the sky, and can be removed.

The methods are shamatha (calm abiding), which stabilizes attention; vipashyana (special insight), which investigates the mind’s nature; lojong (mind training), which turns difficulties into practice; and analytical meditation on dependent origination, emptiness, and impermanence.

Ganden Lha Gyema

Ganden Lha gyema (also written Ganden La Gyama) is a lineage prayer in the Geluk tradition. Its name, meaning “the hundred Ganden,” refers to the lineage of Ganden, the monastery founded by Je Tsongkhapa. The prayer calls on the successive teachers of the Ganden lineage, gathering their blessings into the practitioner’s mind.

It is recited in Geluk monasteries and centres, often in the morning or at special occasions, as a form of guru yoga. Practitioners visualize the lineage masters above their heads and request their guidance and blessings. Recitation is said to strengthen devotion, connect the practice to the living lineage, and support the study of Lamrim.

The prayer is valued because it joins the teachings to the teachers who preserved them. Practitioners recite it with the intention of receiving the lineage’s wisdom and compassion, and of carrying that understanding into daily life.

Acharya Shantideva’s A Guide to the Bodhisattva’s Way of Life

Bodhicaryavatara is one of the most widely read works in Mahayana Buddhism. Shantideva, an 8th-century Indian monk associated with Nalanda monastery, wrote it in about 900 verses in ten chapters. It describes how to develop bodhicitta, the wish to attain awakening for the benefit of all beings, and how to practise the bodhisattva path in daily life.

The lamrim tradition

Lamrim means “stages of the path.” The genre begins with the Indian master Atisha’s Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment(Bodhipathapradipa, 1042), which presents the whole Buddhist path as a graded progression. Tsongkhapa drew on that model and on the wider Kadampa teachings to organise the Buddha’s teachings into a single, sequenced practice, so that each stage prepares the mind for the next.

description:
Middle Length Lamrim
by Je Tsongkhapa | Taught by Venerable Gyalten Lekden
Saturday Evening Teachings

The Middle Length Lamrim (Lam-rim chen-mo 'bring) is one of the great masterworks of Tibetan Buddhism, composed by Je Tsongkhapa (1357–1419), the founder of the Gelug tradition. Written as a more compact companion to his monumental Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path, it distills centuries of Indian and Tibetan wisdom into a clear, practical roadmap — the "stages of the path" (lam-rim) that lead a practitioner from the very first steps of Dharma practice all the way to full enlightenment. Drawing on the lineage of Atisha's Lamp for the Path, Tsongkhapa's text weaves together sutra and tantra, philosophy and meditation, into a single unified structure that generations of practitioners have relied on ever since.

Each Saturday evening, this rich text comes alive under the guidance of Venerable Gyalten Lekden, whose warm and thorough teaching style makes the profound accessible — grounding ancient philosophy in the practicalities of everyday life and meditation practice. Students are led step by step through the path, building both understanding and the motivation to put it into practice.

Whether you are new to the Lamrim or returning to deepen your study, all are warmly welcome to join.

APPEARANCE AND REALITY IN BUDDHIST THOUGHT 

Zoom Link: https://us02web.zoom.us/j/8105820312?pwd=shSzand46dda8xqKYrPgBPUPPQa7kj.1

Zoom Login: 8105820312

Passcode: karuna

Appearance and reality in Buddhist thought

The question of how things appear and how they actually exist is central to Buddhist philosophy. The Madhyamaka tradition, which Tsongkhapa’s Gelug school follows, addresses it through the two truths:

  • Conventional truth (kun rdzob bden pa) is the way things appear and function in everyday experience. A table holds a cup, a person acts and has a name. These appearances are valid for practical purposes.
  • Ultimate truth (don dam bden pa) is the way things actually exist. Phenomena lack inherent, independent existence and are empty of it. This is emptiness, the final nature of phenomena.

About Geshe Tenzin Namdak

Geshe Tenzin Namdak is a Dutch-born Tibetan Buddhist teacher, and he is the resident teacher at Jamyang Buddhist Centre in London. I’m assuming he is the Geshe Tenzin Namdak on your schedule, but please confirm that before the write-up goes out.

Background

  • He trained in hydrology in the Netherlands and worked as an environmental researcher before becoming a monk.
  • He began Buddhist study at the Maitreya Institute in the Netherlands.
  • He was ordained by the Dalai Lama.
  • He spent over 20 years at Sera Jey Monastic University in India, completing the traditional Geshe degree. He is described as one of the first Westerners to do so.
  • He also completed the one-year Vajrayana programme at Gyume Tantric College.
  • He was a student of Lama Zopa Rinpoche.

Teaching and work

  • He is the resident teacher at Jamyang Buddhist Centre London, which is affiliated with FPMT. He leads courses and puja services, all in English, and teaches internationally.
  • He is an Associate Tutor on the Buddhist Mind Science programme at Oxford University.
  • He takes part in Science & Wisdom dialogues with scientists.
  • He worked in the Sera Jey Translation Department on Khedrup Je’s commentary on Dharmakirti’s Seven Treatises on Valid Cognition, published as Freedom Through Correct Knowing.
  • His teaching covers Buddhist philosophy, lojong (mind training) and lamrim, with texts by Nagarjuna, Atisha, Shantideva and Je Tsongkhapa.

description:
Tara Practice

Tara (Tibetan Drolma, “the one who liberates”) is a female bodhisattva who is widely honoured in Tibetan Buddhism. She is known as a swift protector who helps practitioners overcome fears and obstacles, both outer and inner, and who supports them on the path to awakening.

Who Tara is

Tibetan tradition describes Tara as arising from a tear of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, and as the embodiment of his compassionate activity. She appears in many forms. The two most common in practice are Green Tara, associated with swift action and protection, and White Tara, associated with long life, healing and peace. Tara is also a deity of the Tantric path, and in Tibetan practice she is often approached as a meditational deity (yidam) whose qualities the practitioner gradually takes on.

What the practice involves

Tara practice usually includes:

  • Refuge and generating bodhicitta, the motivation to benefit all beings.
  • Visualisation of Tara in front of oneself, radiating light and blessing the practitioner.
  • Recitation of Tara’s mantra, most commonly OM TARE TUTTARE TURE SOHA.
  • Praise and offerings, often the Praises to the Twenty-One Taras (Drolma Chudrug), a widely used text that praises her many qualities and enlightened activities.
  • Dedication of merit at the end, so that the benefit extends to all beings.

Practitioners often do Tara practice for protection, for removing obstacles, for healing and for the wellbeing of others. In the Gelug tradition it is commonly practised as a group puja, with chanting led by a teacher.

At CKSL

The Tara Practice is on Saturday, 28 November, 6 to 8 pm, online. Archana Bharatee leads it. It is listed under Puja in the schedule. The October programme also included a Tara teaching, “Who is Tara and the Benefits of Relying on Tara”, followed by the practice.

That training shapes his teaching: he approaches the Dharma with careful reasoning, and he expects his students to think through what they hear rather than simply accept it.

His teaching centres on the Lamrim, the graded stages of the path to enlightenment composed by Je Tsongkhapa. The Lamrim moves step by step from the preciousness of human life, through impermanence, karma, and the suffering of cyclic existence, to renunciation, the awakening of compassion, and the wisdom that realizes emptiness. Geshe Tenzin Zopa’s approach is to show how these stages build on one another, so that a student understands not only what to practise but why each practice leads to the next.

A recurring theme in his teaching is the relationship between study and meditation. Understanding the view intellectually is not enough, and meditation without understanding can drift into vagueness. He encourages students to hold both together: to study with a clear mind, and to meditate on what they have studied until it becomes part of their experience. This makes his teaching accessible to newcomers, who are given a solid foundation, and valuable to experienced practitioners, who are invited to examine familiar ideas more closely.

Those who attend his teachings often describe them as clear, patient, and grounded in daily life. He draws on the classical sources while relating them to the ordinary difficulties of work, family, and emotion, so that the Dharma feels usable rather than remote.

Acharya Shantideva’s A Guide to the Bodhisattva’s Way of Life

Bodhicaryavatara is one of the most widely read works in Mahayana Buddhism. Shantideva, an 8th-century Indian monk associated with Nalanda monastery, wrote it in about 900 verses in ten chapters. It describes how to develop bodhicitta, the wish to attain awakening for the benefit of all beings, and how to practise the bodhisattva path in daily life.
